summary: Presents extensions to RSVP for generic policy-based admission control, letting policy information be carried along with reservation requests. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: RSVP reserves bandwidth for a flow, but it only checks whether the bandwidth is there. This RFC adds a way for a network to carry policy decisions along with the reservation, so that a flow can also be refused for a reason that has nothing to do with capacity.

subtitle: How RSVP carries policy information in POLICY_DATA objects so admission control can consider more than free bandwidth.

tldr.problem: RSVP gives some users better service than others, yet the base RSVP admission control looks only at resource availability, with no standard way to carry access or usage policy.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2750 defines the format of the POLICY_DATA object and its options, rules for how RSVP nodes forward, refresh, expire and report errors on policy data, and an optional INTEGRITY object for policy nodes that are not neighbours.
tldr.outcome: RSVP messages can carry opaque policy elements between policy-capable nodes, even across nodes that know nothing about policy. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2205.

today: RFC 2750 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2000. It updates RFC 2205, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The framework it builds on is RFC 2753, and the protocol for talking to a policy decision point is RFC 2748.

sections.title: Why RSVP Needs Policy Control
sections.content:
RSVP, by definition, treats users differently, by giving some of them better service at the expense of others. It is therefore reasonable to expect RSVP to come with mechanisms for controlling and enforcing access and usage policies. Version 1 of the RSVP functional specification left a placeholder for policy support in the form of a POLICY_DATA object.

The RSVP functional specification describes the interface to admission control, which is traffic control, based only on resource availability. This document describes a set of extensions to RSVP that support policy-based admission control as well. The scope is limited to those extensions, and the RFC does not advocate a particular architecture for policy-based control. It also does not distinguish between a Policy Decision Point and a Local Decision Point as described in RFC 2753; the term Policy Decision Point is used to include the local decision point as well.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP can only say yes or no based on how much capacity is free. This RFC gives it a way to carry a second kind of answer, one based on policy.

sections.title: The Scenario: PEPs and PINs
sections.content:
Policy enforcement, at least in its early stages, is likely to concentrate on the border nodes between autonomous systems. The RFC's example has an autonomous domain with two boundary nodes, A and C, which are policy enforcement points (PEPs) controlled by policy decision points (PDP1 and PDP2), and a core node B that is RSVP capable but policy ignorant, called a policy ignorant node (PIN), with capabilities limited to default policy handling.

In that example the policy objects travel across the domain through the PIN node B, which is allowed to process RSVP messages but is not trusted to handle policy information. The RFC therefore gives processing rules for both kinds of node, the PEP and the PIN.

POLICY_DATA objects are carried by RSVP messages, and any policy-capable node, wherever it sits, can generate, modify or remove them, even when the sender and the receiver neither provide nor know about policy data objects. Exchanging them along the data path supports a consistent end-to-end policy, and lets such a policy be deployed across several administrative domains, where the border nodes manipulate and translate the objects according to bilateral agreements.
sections.plainLanguage: The policy decisions are made at the edges of the network by a separate control system, and the rules travel inside the RSVP messages. A core router that understands nothing about policy just passes them along.

sections.title: The POLICY_DATA Object
sections.content:
POLICY_DATA is an RSVP object of class 14, and this RFC defines the type 1 object, with C-Type 1. Its header holds a Length field, the object type and C-Type, a 16-bit Data Offset, and a 16-bit reserved field that is always zero. The Data Offset is the offset in bytes of the data portion, counted from the first byte of the object header.

After the header come two variable-length lists. The Option List holds the options described in the next section. The Policy Element List holds the policy elements, whose contents are opaque to RSVP: only the policy peers, such as a policy decision point, understand their internal format, and their codepoints are kept in a registry.

Each policy element has its own small header: a Length field and a P-Type, followed by policy information that is opaque to RSVP.
sections.plainLanguage: The object has a short header, then a list of options that control how the object is handled, then a list of policy elements that hold the actual decisions.

sections.title: Options Inside POLICY_DATA
sections.content:
Five options are defined. A FILTER_SPEC object, or a SCOPE object, describes the set of senders the policy applies to; if neither is given, the policy is assumed to apply to all the flows of the session, and the two are mutually exclusive. The SCOPE object is used to prevent policy loops, because the RSVP SCOPE object cannot do that when a policy ignorant node is part of a wildcard flow reservation path. Using it can have a significant effect on the size and scaling of the objects.

The originating RSVP_HOP identifies the neighbouring policy-capable node that built the policy object, and it is the basis for the mechanism that lets policy nodes several RSVP hops apart recognize each other and talk directly and safely. If it is absent, the policy data is assumed to have been built by the RSVP_HOP of the message itself. A second, destination RSVP_HOP, may follow and identifies the policy node the object is aimed at, which ensures delivery to the targeted policy nodes, can emulate unicast delivery in multicast Path messages, and helps prevent a policy object being used elsewhere in the network, which is a replay attack. A receiving policy node should ignore any POLICY_DATA whose destination RSVP_HOP does not match its own IP address.

The INTEGRITY object option creates a direct secure channel between policy enforcement points that are not neighbours, without involving the policy ignorant nodes in between, and is computed as described in Appendix B of the RFC. The Policy Refresh TIME_VALUES (PRT) option slows the policy refresh rate for policies with looser timing constraints than RSVP itself. The refresh multiplier is N = Floor(PRT/R), and both the refresh and the state cleanup are slowed by that factor, although the multiplier applies only to periodic no-change refreshes and not to updates. The option is also useful for combining strong and weak authentication certificates, where the weak one admits a reservation only for a limited time.
sections.plainLanguage: The options say which flows the policy applies to, which node built it, which node should get it, how to protect it, and how often it has to be refreshed.

sections.title: Policy Elements and Policy State
sections.content:
Policy state expires in the granularity of policy elements, because the POLICY_DATA objects are mere containers and do not expire as such. A policy element expires in exactly the same manner and at the same time as the RSVP state received in the same message, and state controlled by the PRT option expires N times more slowly.

Only one policy element of a given P-Type can be active at a time. A policy element is therefore replaced at once when another element of the same P-Type arrives from the same policy decision point, whether that is the previous or the next policy RSVP hop. An empty policy element of a given P-Type is used to delete all the policy state of that P-Type, rather than to replace it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece of policy has its own lifetime and its own name, and a new piece with the same name replaces the old one. An empty piece deletes the state instead.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
Policy control is enforced for Path, Resv, PathErr and ResvErr messages only. PathTear and ResvTear are assumed not to need it, on two grounds: that integrity verification guarantees the tear came from the node that sent the installed reservation, and that this is functionally equivalent to that node holding off refreshes for the reservation.

A policy ignorant node has a minimum duty, which is to forward the POLICY_DATA objects it receives in the appropriate outgoing messages. The objects are forwarded as they are, without modification. At a node that merges or splits multicast, the rule upstream is that when several POLICY_DATA objects arrive from downstream they are concatenated as a list of the original objects and forwarded with the outgoing message; downstream, when a single object arrives from upstream it is copied to all the downstream branches of the tree. The same rules apply to unrecognized policies inside a POLICY_DATA object, though that can only happen in a policy-capable node, so it is the responsibility of the policy decision point and not of RSVP.
sections.plainLanguage: Policy control applies to the four messages that set up and fail reservations. A node that does not understand policy still has to pass the policy objects along unchanged, and handle multicast branching correctly.

sections.title: Integrity and Security
sections.content:
Two security mechanisms can be used, both optional, to keep the carried information intact. The first relies on the RSVP integrity mechanism of RFC 2747 to provide a chain of trust when every RSVP node is policy capable. The second relies on the INTEGRITY object inside the POLICY_DATA object, and it guarantees integrity between policy enforcement points that are not neighbours of each other.

The second mechanism exists because the RSVP integrity mechanism becomes ineffective in the scenario of the RFC's example, where policy objects travel between boundary nodes across policy ignorant nodes: the RSVP mechanism places policy trust with those intermediate nodes, which are trusted to perform RSVP signalling but not to make policy decisions or to manipulate policy objects. The INTEGRITY option creates a direct secure channel between the non-neighbouring policy enforcement points and their policy decision points, without involving the policy ignorant nodes. It is used at the discretion of the policy decision points, and Appendix B of the RFC sets out how it is computed.
sections.plainLanguage: The normal RSVP protection only works if every node on the path is trusted, which a core router that only forwards policy is not. The INTEGRITY option protects the policy objects directly between the nodes that make the decisions.

sections.title: Policy Error Codes
sections.content:
Policy errors are reported with ResvErr or PathErr messages carrying a policy failure error code in the ERROR_SPEC object, which is class 6 with error code 02. The error message must include a POLICY_DATA object that holds the details of the error type and the reason in a format specific to the P-Type.

If a multicast reservation fails for policy reasons, RSVP should not try to work out which reservation caused the failure, as it would for a blockade state. It should try to deliver the policy ResvErr to all the downstream hops and let the policy decision point decide where the messages should go. That lets the policy decision point limit the error distribution by choosing which next hops to inform, and it lets it stop further distribution of the error by repairing the problem locally, for instance by substituting a different POLICY_DATA object.

Appendix A of the RFC lists the error values, which run from 0, ERR_INFO for information reporting, to 19, ERR_FL_SPEC for a rejected flow specification. Values between 2^15 and 2^16-1 are for site or vendor use.
sections.plainLanguage: When a policy refuses a reservation, the error travels in the normal RSVP error message, with a policy failure code and a policy object that explains the reason.
